source: Schoenfeld (1982) Expert and Novice Mathematical Problem Solving, NSF final report (describes the 1979 lab study)
finding: Describes Schoenfeld's 1979 controlled lab study. Two groups of students trained for identical time on identical problems and saw the same solutions. Only one group also saw the heuristics behind each solution. The no-heuristics group could not use their problem experience on related problems. The heuristics group used the heuristics explicitly.
numbers: Report says 'significant difference in performance'; no group size or test statistic in this report. ERIC record of the 1979 JRME paper says it covers seven upper-division college students.
quote: the journey from the laboratory to the classroom is a long one
limits: Lab study only. Full 1979 JRME paper was not accessible this session.
agent_relevance: Experience alone does not teach heuristics; the solution must be shown WITH the named strategy behind it. Supports putting an explicit strategy name next to each worked step in prompts.

source: Schoenfeld (1979) Explicit heuristic training as a variable in problem-solving performance, JRME 10(3) (ERIC record EJ202121)
finding: Abstract only: seven upper-division college students worked problems solvable with one or more heuristics; their processes were described in detail.
numbers: N=7 (per ERIC abstract).
limits: Abstract only, read via the ERIC API. Tiny sample, process description rather than a large controlled trial.
agent_relevance: The founding 'training helps' result is a small-N, process-level study. Treat it as a mechanism hint, not a strong effect size.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) final report: classroom problem-solving course study
finding: Second study was in a classroom with replicable measures. Students were taught heuristics AND a managerial strategy together, so the two effects cannot be separated. Heuristic fluency became much greater and correlated with dramatically improved problem solving.
numbers: No N or test statistics in this summary paragraph. The same report gives the measured course effect in the card-sort study: see a07.
limits: Confounded: heuristics and management taught together. Schoenfeld calls some related before-after data 'shaky'.
agent_relevance: Heuristics are never tested alone in the classic work. Our control layer (states and operators) mirrors the combination that did work.

source: Schoenfeld (1978) Presenting a strategy for indefinite integration (as cited in the 1982 report)
finding: Students who already knew integration techniques were split. Controls studied the usual way. The experimental group got a strategy for SELECTING which technique to use. The experimental group studied less and did better.
numbers: Control averaged 9 hours of study, strategy group 7 hours; strategy group 'significantly outperformed' controls (no statistic in the report).
limits: Second-hand summary in the 1982 report; narrow domain; a selection strategy, not Polya-type heuristics.
agent_relevance: A small decision procedure for choosing between known tools saved time and raised accuracy. This is the pattern our program-controlled operator choice relies on.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) final report, introduction: state of the evidence on heuristics
finding: Schoenfeld says there was little conclusive evidence that heuristics work, in the sense that students learn them AND improve. Earlier studies found students could master single strategies, but the overall gain was far below hopes (Wilson 1967; Smith 1973; Lucas and Loomer 1980; Goldberg 1975). He hypothesises that heuristics alone are not sufficient and that weak management wastes them.
numbers: Cites four prior studies by name; gives no effect sizes.
quote: the problem solving whole was, somehow, less than the sum of its heuristic parts
limits: Secondary description by an interested author; the cited studies were not opened.
agent_relevance: Core reason for our scaffold: a heuristic list without a control layer gives weak transfer. Matches schema section 4b (do not just add strategies).

source: Schoenfeld (1983) Theoretical and pragmatic issues in the design of mathematical problem solving instruction (ERIC ED228045)
finding: Framework of three categories: resources (facts, algorithms, local heuristics), control (monitoring, assessment, decisions) and belief systems. Heuristics sit inside resources; domain-specific forms are like schemata ('draw a figure' resembles 'look for congruent triangles'). His early course was 'cognitive engineering': model the expert, train students to match. It passed an 'acid test' of gains on unrelated problems, but videotapes of strong students (calculus B or better) showed deep anti-mathematical beliefs.
numbers: In a geometry construction task, no pair of students reasoned to a solution; they guessed constructions for 15 to 20 minutes with compass in hand. Only one pair justified afterwards, and only empirically.
limits: Theory paper with protocol examples; the course test is cited to Schoenfeld 1982 and not shown here.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our schema: resources = operators, control = program-run states, beliefs = guardrails. Knowing a fact (proof, geometry) does not mean using it unless control triggers it.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) final report: problem-perception card-sort experiment (course vs programming control vs experts)
finding: Pre/post design. Eleven students took a month-long problem-solving course (heuristic and executive strategies). Eight took a month-long programming course as control. Nine math professors sorted once. After the course, only the problem-solving group improved on problem-solving tests and sorted problems by deep structure more like experts.
numbers: N: 11 course, 8 control, 9 experts. Mean test score course group 21 -> 73; control 14 -> 24. ANOVA: term F(1,17)=47.5 p<.001; group F(1,17)=130.6 p<.001; interaction F(1,17)=48.2 p<.001. Experts' 22 strongly clustered pairs: 13 (.59) shared surface structure, 18 (.82) shared deep structure; among 12 conflicting pairs, .25 surface vs .67 deep.
limits: Small N; course group enrolled by choice and unpaid, controls paid $20 and not randomised. Course taught heuristics plus executive control plus beliefs, so effect cannot be assigned to heuristics alone.
agent_relevance: The one clean large pre-post effect in the founding work. A scaffold that bundles heuristics, control and belief-like rules is what moved scores.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) final report: pre/post protocols (executive behaviour)
finding: Before the course, pairs jumped into one approach and rarely stopped it ('proof by assumption', the assistants' name). Little was salvaged from a bad first try. After the course there was more evaluation and curtailment of other approaches and fewer wild goose chases.
numbers: Pretest jumping 'pretty much the norm'. Only two of the twelve posttest protocols showed the bad pattern (scope of 'that type' unclear in the extract).
limits: Qualitative coding by Schoenfeld and assistants; 12 posttest protocols.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and the impasse detector: the fix is not more ideas but curtailing a failing line. Our code-run budget check per attempt does this externally.

source: Lucas (1972/1974) Teaching of heuristic problem-solving strategies in elementary calculus, JRME / ERIC ED072940
finding: Solomon four-group design in two calculus classes. The heuristic-oriented group beat the no-heuristics group on approach, plan and result scores. They hesitated less, solved slightly faster and spent much more time checking results.
numbers: N=30 students in two classes; Solomon four-group; no statistic in abstract.
limits: Abstract only (full text returned HTML). Interview-based scoring, small N, one class per condition.
agent_relevance: Gains showed in plan quality and checking time, which are control behaviours. Argues for scoring plan and verify steps, not just final answers.

source: Charles and Lester (1984) An evaluation of a process-oriented instructional program in mathematical problem solving in grades 5 and 7, JRME
finding: 46 teachers in grades 5 and 7. Classes using the problem-solving program scored significantly higher than control classes on understanding problems, planning solution strategies and getting correct answers. Growth patterns and attitudes differed.
numbers: 46 teachers; significance reported, no effect sizes in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Program taught as a package.
agent_relevance: Largest classic field trial where gains split into understand, plan, answer. Matches our state split (restate, plan, execute).

source: Hembree (1992) Experiments and relational studies in problem solving: a meta-analysis, JRME 23(3)
finding: Integrated 487 reports. Problem solving related positively to basic skills. Teachers trained in heuristic methods had positive effects on student performance. Also covered harder and easier problem conditions and classroom conditions.
numbers: 487 reports; effect sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes by treatment type not read. Older studies of mixed quality.
agent_relevance: Best human aggregate that heuristic instruction helps on average. Need the exact d values before citing a number.

source: Kantowski (1977) Processes involved in mathematical problem solving, JRME 8(3)
finding: Clinical exploratory study of 8 ninth graders learning to solve non-routine geometry problems; tracked how their processes changed as heuristic instruction was given.
limits: Abstract only; hypothesis-generating, not a test.
agent_relevance: Source of a coding scheme for heuristic processes (cited by Schoenfeld); useful for tagging agent traces.

source: Liljedahl, Santos-Trigo, Malaspina, Bruder (2016) Problem Solving in Mathematics Education, ICME-13 survey, sections 1.1-1.2
finding: In the 1960s-70s, studies stressed heuristic strategies on the Polya model, mainly in talent programmes, and were 'rather successful' (Sewerin 1979). In the 1980s focus widened to attitudes, emotions, self-regulation. Kilpatrick (1985) listed five promotion methods: osmosis, memorisation, imitation, cooperation, reflection. The debate is now which heuristics and how, not whether to teach them.
numbers: No quantitative effect sizes in this chapter.
limits: Narrative survey. 'Rather successful' refers to selected talent programmes, not regular classes.
agent_relevance: Names the teaching modes we can mimic: imitation = worked traces, reflection = looking-back operator.

source: Mason, Burton, Stacey (1982) Thinking Mathematically (as summarised in Liljedahl et al. 2016, section 1.2.8)
finding: Heuristic built on two processes: specializing (try special cases) and generalizing (find why it works). Phases: entry (get started, get involved), attack (conjecture and test), review (check, reflect, generalise). Being stuck is 'an honourable and positive state'; first step is to write STUCK! then list what is known, wanted, introduced and assumed. Oscillate between entry and attack until an AHA.
numbers: No experimental data. The book is a prescriptive, learner-run course.
quote: an honourable and positive state, from which much can be learned
limits: Secondary summary; the book itself was not read. The method is first-person and reflective, so it needs a learner who can notice being stuck.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete stuck-routine our impasse detector can trigger: list known/wanted/assumed, then specialise. Core gap: no experiments exist for it.

source: Schoenfeld (1985, 1992) as characterised by Liljedahl et al. 2016, sections 1.2.6 and 1.3
finding: Schoenfeld found Polya's heuristics are broad and general and give no clear direction on how learners could assimilate and use them. Students need to discuss what a heuristic means in a concrete case (special cases for series, roots of polynomials). Experts with no schema explore, match to familiar problems, juggle options, back off, and may succeed partly by luck.
numbers: No numbers in this chapter.
limits: Secondary; Polya's own book was not read.
agent_relevance: Why a heuristic name alone does little: the agent needs worked, domain-bound versions of each heuristic.

source: Perkins (2000) four stuck types, as summarised in Liljedahl et al. 2016, section 1.2.7
finding: Perkins says solvable but 'unreasonable' problems leave you stuck in one of four ways: wilderness of possibilities, clueless plateau, narrow canyon, oasis of false promise. Each has a matching exit (search systematically, look for clues in the wording, check for self-imposed constraints, re-attack away from the near answer). The survey notes it is easier to get stuck than to notice being stuck.
numbers: No data.
limits: Prescriptive heuristic with no effect tests in this source.
agent_relevance: A four-way impasse classifier is a cheap diagnostic our code could emit; untested.

source: Koichu, Berman, Moore (2007) The effect of promoting heuristic literacy on the mathematical aptitude of middle-school students, IJMEST
finding: Controlled five-month classroom experiment with 8th graders: heuristic vocabulary and selected heuristics were promoted indirectly. Mean effect size moderate, in line with earlier heuristic research. Students below the sample average at the start gained significantly more than the rest.
numbers: N=92; moderate mean effect size (value not in abstract).
limits: Abstract only. Authors argue the benefit is partly communicational (shared words), not purely cognitive.
agent_relevance: Naming heuristics helps weaker solvers most. Suggests a shared named vocabulary of operators matters for the model too.

source: Hohn and Frey (2002) Heuristic training and performance in elementary mathematical problem solving, J. Educational Research
finding: SOLVED heuristic (translate, interpret, plan, execute, monitor) for upper elementary students. It beat traditional problem-solving instruction on short-term and delayed problem solving. Accuracy correlated significantly with metacognitive processing.
numbers: No N or effect size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. The strategy bundles a monitoring step.
agent_relevance: Another test of a heuristic that includes a monitor step; gains tied to metacognition.

source: Eisenmann, Novotna, Pribyl, Brehovsky (2015) The development of a culture of problem solving with secondary students through heuristic strategies, MERJ
finding: 16-month study of 62 Czech pupils aged 12-18. Pupils improved most in creativity and attitudes. Some heuristics were teachable (systematic experimentation, guess-check-revise, adding an auxiliary element) and some were not, or only with difficulty (specialisation, generalisation, analogy).
numbers: N=62 in three classes; 16 months.
limits: Abstract only; no randomised control mentioned.
agent_relevance: Teachability differs by heuristic. Analogy and generalisation, the most abstract, transfer worst. Do not assume all operators transfer equally.

source: Eisenmann et al. (2015) Impact of heuristic strategies on pupils' attitudes to problem solving, ERIES Journal 8(1)
finding: 11 teaching experiments in ordinary North Bohemian schools (2012-13). Pre/post written tests on problems where a heuristic is most efficient. Success and strategy use rose after teaching, most for easy-to-practise strategies (auxiliary element, systematic experimentation); 'omitting a condition' needed longer.
numbers: 12-year-olds (n=98): kite area success 13% -> 58%, auxiliary-element use 18% -> 74%; inscribed square 9% -> 20%. 14-year-olds (n=109): consecutive odd numbers 21% -> 54%, systematic experimentation use 0% -> 27%. 17-year-olds (n=78): one problem 27% -> 39%. Experiments: 4 + 4 + 3.
limits: No control group; tests are the same style as the training problems (near transfer); attitude change reported by teachers for about half the pupils per class. Authors warn pupils may overuse systematic experimentation instead of equations.
agent_relevance: Large pre-post jumps for taught heuristics on near problems, small on others: transfer is narrow. Also shows an over-application risk.

source: Haenze and Leiss (2022) Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics, Instructional Science
finding: Randomised classroom experiment with three conditions: control tasks; worked examples of fictitious students negotiating a solution (heuristic worked examples); worked examples plus self-explanation prompts. Strategy knowledge improved for grades 5 and 7, but real modelling competency improved only for grade 7. Self-explanation prompts added nothing, and for grade 7 modelling competency they were worse than plain examples.
numbers: N=134 (grade 5) and 180 (grade 7), 45 min each. Grade 7 posttest: modelling competency F(2,174)=5.10 p<.01 partial eta2=.06; strategy knowledge F(2,174)=5.26 p<.01 eta2=.06. Grade 5 strategy knowledge F(2,128)=4.18 p<.05 eta2=.06; grade 5 modelling competency no effect. Follow-up: grade 7 modelling F(2,163)=3.86 p<.05 eta2=.05, strategy knowledge p=.06; grade 5 follow-up not significant.
limits: Single 45-minute session; effects fade at follow-up weeks later; strategy knowledge did not turn into use for the younger pupils.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: knowing a strategy is not applying it. Prompting self-reflection can hurt. Fits G1: no scheduled doubt prompts.

source: Higgins (1993) Effects of a systematic approach to problem solving (Oregon Lane County PSM materials), ERIC ED365521
finding: One year; half of 2 sixth-grade and 4 seventh-grade teachers used heuristic materials (five direct-taught skills, weekly challenges, guided discovery). Heuristic students held fewer memorisation beliefs, expected teachers to ask questions, and relied less on teacher and textbook.
numbers: 6 teachers, one year.
limits: Abstract only. Reported gains are in beliefs and attitudes, not ability scores.
agent_relevance: Heuristic instruction shifts beliefs about maths more than scores; the belief side is the least portable to an LLM.

source: Pereira-Mendoza (1979) Heuristic strategies utilized by high school students, Alberta J. Educational Research
finding: Cases, symmetry and analysis were the heuristics high school students most often used on novel problems. Use of a heuristic appears to be problem-dependent.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Heuristic use depends on the task; a fixed schedule of heuristics will misfire. Supports task-triggered operators.

source: Lein, Jitendra, Harwell (2020) Effectiveness of mathematical word problem solving interventions for students with LD and/or MD: a meta-analysis, J. Educational Psychology
finding: 33 studies, 31 in analysis (34 effect sizes). Word-problem interventions gave a moderate positive effect. Larger for elementary than secondary, researcher-made than normed tests, researcher than teacher implementers. Schema-based TRANSFER instruction beat schema-based instruction, strategy instruction and others.
limits: Word-problem strategy teaching for struggling learners, not general Polya heuristics. Effects shrink on normed tests and with teacher implementers.
agent_relevance: Explicit transfer training is the best arm. Effects shrink on standard measures: a warning for benchmark gains.

source: Myers, Hughes, Witzel, Anderson, Owens (2023) Meta-analysis of math interventions for word-problem solving, grades 4-12, J. Research on Educational Effectiveness
finding: 36 studies (1989-2020), 88 outcomes. Overall effect large and positive. Effect varied by intervention model, interventionist, grade, topic and duration; no design feature moderated. A companion article (Witzel and Myers 2023, ERIC EJ1402391) names Schema-Based Instruction and General Heuristics Instruction as the two effective strategies for secondary students with learning disabilities.
limits: Mixes many interventions; population is students with maths difficulties.
agent_relevance: Recent human meta-analysis where general heuristics instruction survives; population-limited.

source: Zhang and Xin (2012) follow-up meta-analysis of word-problem interventions for students with maths difficulties, J. Educational Research (and Xin and Jitendra 1999)
finding: 29 group-design and 10 single-subject studies, 1996-2009. Overall effect positive. Xin and Jitendra (1999) earlier found, over 25 studies, long-term interventions larger than short-term and computer-assisted instruction strongest in group designs.
numbers: Group designs mean weighted d = 1.848; single-subject PND = 95%.
limits: Very large d suggests researcher-made tests and weak controls; not general heuristics.
agent_relevance: Shows inflation risk: large d on narrow custom tests; do not quote as expected benchmark gain.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models, ICLR
finding: Polya-style decomposition (solve easier subproblems first, reuse their answers). Huge win on compositional length generalisation (SCAN), small win on grade-school math. Gain grows with the number of steps in the solution.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: least-to-most 99.7%, chain-of-thought 16.2%, standard 16.7% (14 exemplars). GSM8K: least-to-most 62.39% vs CoT 60.87%. GSM8K by steps: 5+ steps 45.23% vs 39.07%; 2 steps 74.53% vs 76.68%. DROP non-football 82.45 vs 74.77; football 73.42 vs 59.56. Last-letter length 12: CoT with 4 or 8 independent exemplars 37.4% / 38.4%.
limits: Old GPT-3 family models; hand-designed prompts per task; text-davinci-002 CoT scored 0.0 on SCAN; on 2-step GSM8K problems least-to-most was slightly worse than CoT.
agent_relevance: Decomposition helps where subproblems are real and steps are many; on short problems it can hurt. Gate it on a step-count signal.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting, ACL
finding: Zero-shot 'devise a plan then carry it out' (PS) and a version that also says extract variables and watch calculation (PS+). Beats 'let's think step by step' on six math sets; PS+ about matches 8-shot manual CoT on average.
numbers: text-davinci-003 GSM8K: zero-shot CoT 56.4 -> PS+ 59.3 (+2.9); other math sets at least +5. Average of six math sets: PS+ 76.7 vs manual 8-shot CoT 77.6 and Auto-CoT 75.9. CSQA 71.9 vs 65.2 zero-shot CoT; StrategyQA 65.4 vs 63.8. Error analysis of GSM8K: zero-shot CoT wrong on 46 of 100 sampled (calculation 7%, missing step 12%, semantic 27%); PS 43 wrong; PS+ 39 wrong (calculation 5%, missing step 7%, semantic similar to CoT).
limits: One model (GPT-3), greedy decode, 2023. The plan fixes missing steps and arithmetic, not misunderstanding, the biggest category.
agent_relevance: A plan-first step is a cheap Polya step 2. It cuts missing-step and calculation errors but not comprehension errors; those need the restate operator and checks.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction in LLMs, ICLR
finding: Two-step prompt: first ask for the high-level principle or concept, then reason from it (akin to Polya's 'think of a more general related problem'). Large gains on physics, chemistry, temporal and multi-hop QA. Plain CoT often did not help PaLM-2L.
numbers: PaLM-2L MMLU Physics 66.4% -> 73.2% (CoT 65%); Chemistry 70.9% -> 81.8% (CoT 75.3%). GPT-4 Physics 69.4 -> 84.5 (CoT 82.9); Chemistry 80.9 -> 85.6 (CoT 85.3). TimeQA PaLM-2L 41.5% -> 66% (with RAG 68.7%). MuSiQue: GPT-4 38.5% vs step-back PaLM-2L 42.8%; StrategyQA 86.4%.
limits: Gains largest on knowledge-heavy tasks; one exemplar suffices; on GPT-4 the Physics gain over CoT is only 1.6 points and Chemistry 0.3.
agent_relevance: Abstraction is nearly free and works as a heuristic operator, but on strong models the gain over CoT is small. Test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: error analysis
finding: Where step-back still fails: more than 90% of its errors happen in the reasoning step, not in the abstraction step. On MMLU high-school Physics it fixes 20.5% of baseline errors while introducing 11.9% new ones.
numbers: Principle errors are a small fraction; reasoning and math errors dominate the five error classes (principle, factual, math, context loss, reasoning).
limits: Annotated errors on one benchmark with one model.
agent_relevance: A good heuristic cannot fix execution errors, and the 11.9% new-error rate shows a heuristic can break items the base model got right. Track both directions.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs self-compose reasoning structures
finding: The model selects from a set of atomic reasoning modules, adapts them to the task, and writes a JSON reasoning structure, then follows it. Beats direct, CoT and Plan-and-Solve on hard sets, with far less inference than sampling methods.
numbers: PaLM 2-L: BBH 56 direct, 60 CoT, 61 PS, 67 Self-Discover; T4D 30/40/42/69; MATH (200 sampled) 45/42/49/50.5. GPT-4: BBH 58/75/73/81; T4D 51/52/53/85; MATH 70.5/71/70/73. Abstract: up to 32% over CoT; 10-40x less inference compute than self-consistency-style methods. On MATH, 74.7% of failures were computation errors.
limits: Meta-prompts are model-run; no code checks; MATH gain on GPT-4 only 2.5 points over direct; benefit concentrated in world-knowledge and agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that SELECTING among named reasoning strategies per task beats one fixed strategy. Our program could do the selection and the model only fill it. MATH is the weak spot.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners, COLM
finding: Four human-like habits (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) predict whether a base model improves under RL on Countdown. Qwen-2.5-3B has them naturally; Llama-3.2-3B does not. Priming Llama with synthetic traces showing these habits closes the gap.
numbers: After RL Qwen reaches about 60% on Countdown, Llama about 30%. Primed Llama matches or exceeds Qwen. A behaviour-enriched OpenWebMath continued pre-training set also raised Llama toward Qwen.
limits: One task (Countdown) and two 3B models; first priming used task-specific data; the math pretraining set is a second step.
agent_relevance: Named strategies (Polya-like subgoal and backward chaining) are causal for later gains from RL. Supports encoding them explicitly rather than hoping they emerge.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) control conditions (empty and incorrect traces)
finding: Giving Llama empty or length-matched empty chains of thought (extra tokens, no behaviours) left it at base level, and training on empty CoT hurt Qwen. Priming with traces that show the behaviours but reach WRONG answers still enabled improvement.
numbers: Empty-CoT priming 30-35%, same as base Llama. Incorrect-answer traces with behaviours: still improved RL (value in Figure 6, not extracted).
quote: suggesting that cognitive behaviors matter more than solution accuracy
limits: Countdown only; authors say it extends earlier work on learning from corrupted trajectories.
agent_relevance: Extra tokens alone do nothing; the strategy pattern matters. Contrast with arXiv 2605.08472 (a34), where wrong approaches hurt.

source: RRV et al. (2026) Mid-training with self-generated data improves RL in language models (Polya-guided heuristic variants), arXiv 2605.08472
finding: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct is prompted with Polya-style heuristics (analogy, decomposing, bright idea, etc.; up to 64 variants per question) on 7,112 GSM8K questions. Only correct, heuristic-faithful solutions are kept for fine-tuning, then GRPO. More heuristics gives higher pass@k after RL, especially at large k and on hard sets.
numbers: Pass@1 average 9.25% (n=1 heuristic) -> 11.50% (n=64); STaR 13.02% (+1.94 over zero-shot). Pass@64 average: zero-shot 46.30%, STaR 46.32%, n=64 48.17%. After RL, pass@64 average: vanilla RL 44.21%, STaR+RL 45.69%, mid-trained 48.09% (n=16) and 47.62% (n=64). MATH-500 pass@64 83.42% vs 86.27%; AIME 2025 16.91% -> 23.34%; AMC 2023 78.18% -> 84.52%. Qwen2.5-7B: best n=8 17.06%/50.50% vs zero-shot 18.47%/51.39% (no gain).
limits: Training-time method, not a prompt; pass@1 gain is smaller than plain STaR; the stronger Qwen base showed no gain; arXiv preprint.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of teaching Polya heuristics. Benefit appears as diversity (pass@k), not single-shot accuracy. A scaffold with a code-run verifier matches this; G4 warns same-model samples are correlated.

source: RRV et al. (2026) arXiv 2605.08472: ablations on correctness and breadth vs depth
finding: At the same training size, learning many approaches on fewer problems beat one solution on many problems by about 7% relative. When the Polya-style approaches led to WRONG answers, adding more heuristics did not help RL and pass@k fell below vanilla RL on all six benchmarks.
numbers: Average relative gain about 7% for multi-approach vs single-solution mid-training. Incorrect-answer variant: below vanilla RL on all six benchmarks.
limits: Llama-3.2-3B, GSM8K seed; one lab.
agent_relevance: Strategy diversity only helps when each strategy reaches a verified answer. Matches G2 and G3: heuristics without a check are harmful.

source: Lee et al. (2026) Llama-Polya: instruction tuning of an LLM based on Polya's problem solving, arXiv 2602.10597
finding: Llama-3.1-8B tuned on about 32,000 synthetic tutoring dialogues in Polya's four stages (built from GSM8K), compared with base, general instruct and MetaMath variants. Polya-tuned and MetaMath models gave more balanced stage coverage across arithmetic, measurement, geometry and fewer premature direct answers. Expert raters saw better metacognitive prompting.
numbers: About 32,000 dialogue samples; stage-annotation error rate polya-v2 0.0%, metamath 0.4%; base and instruct had higher error rates.
limits: No answer-accuracy benchmark in the text read; evaluated by stage annotation and expert opinion; authors admit limits in personalisation and mathematical rigor.
agent_relevance: Shows models can be made to follow Polya stages, but not that following the stages raises correctness. Stage conformity is not accuracy.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning, ICLR
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus 20 datasets x 14 models. CoT (the base 'show your steps' heuristic) helps mostly on math, symbolic and logic tasks; elsewhere gains are tiny.
numbers: Mean CoT gain: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points; top three categories 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Other categories 56.8 vs 56.1. GSM8K and MATH gains up to 66.9 and 41.6 points on some models. On MMLU, CoT helps almost only if an equals sign appears.
quote: We do not consider this small improvement a victory for CoT.
limits: Prompt-level CoT only.
agent_relevance: Heuristic prompts are task-type specific. Our router should turn step-by-step scaffolds on for symbolic items and off elsewhere.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) planning versus execution split
finding: Separating 'make a plan' from 'carry it out' on math and logic: a plan with a direct answer gains little; most gain comes from tracking execution. A symbolic solver beats both CoT and Plan+CoT in most settings.
numbers: Compared direct, Plan+Direct solver, Plan+CoT solver and Plan+Tool solver on GSM8K and logic sets across models; Plan+Tool best in most settings (exact values in figure 6 and appendix H, not extracted).
limits: Plans are model-written programs or formal specs; some plans were unparseable (rates in appendix).
agent_relevance: Planning heuristics (Polya step 2) are cheap, but code execution gives the gain. Let the program run the plan.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with LLMs, NeurIPS
finding: Keeps a meta-buffer of reusable high-level thought templates (distilled heuristics) and instantiates the best one per task. Claims gains over prior prompting on 10 tasks at about single-query cost.
numbers: Over Meta-prompting: +23% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One (summary line says 11%, 20%, 51%). With GPT-4 as baseline, +79.4% on Game of 24 and +8.4% over Tree of Thoughts.
limits: Templates distilled by the same model; method authors' own claims against a GPT-4 baseline; not independently replicated here; the paper's text gives 23% and 11% for Game of 24 in two places.
agent_relevance: A heuristic library retrieved by task type is the closest LLM analogue of teaching heuristics; needs an independent run at equal tokens before we rely on it.
